Question: What are some realistic improvements that can be made to airline travel?

Question: How much does it cost an airline to provide in-flight wifi? Do airlines charge for it because it’s expensive, because they know people will pay for it, or both?
Answer: The price of a product or service in a competitive marketplace is only partially influenced by the cost to provide the product or service. In the case of inflight wifi the price is dictated by the value of wifi in the eyes of the purchaser. Consider a business traveler on a five hour flight. Paying $29 for five hours of internet connectivity is completely reasonable. The idea that a product or service is expensive is somewhat objective (when you can compare it to substitute products or services) and somewhat subjective (when you’re purchasing a veblen good for example). Airlines operate to generate profit. They’re objective is to maximize profit. Sometimes this means they a sell high volume of goods at a lower profit margin (discount airlines) and sometimes this means they sell a lower volume of goods at a much higher profit margin (private jets). Most airlines partner with wifi providers like Boingo and GogoInFlight. Interesting side note: Boingo’s Nasdaq ticker symbol is wifi. The airlines work with their partners to determine the fee that will result in maximum profit and a good wifi experience for their customers. If the price of the wifi were very low, or even free, hundreds of people could and would attempt to connect to the low bandwidth wifi—resulting in a poor user experience and a dissatisfied customer. -KJ

Question: What are things to note when looking for a business partner?
Answer: What they say is true: a business partnership is like marriage. Complementary Skill Set Your business partner should have a complimentary skillset. EG. if you’re an engineer find someone with sales and marketing skills. We tend to attract and want to partner with people just like ourselves. Resist that temptation and expand the breadth of skills of your leadership. Different Backgrounds & Life Experiences We tend to surround ourselves with people just like us. Integrity No explanation needed here. Integrity is a fundamental characteristic. Without you will fail, your partner will screw you, you’ll get sued, and you may end up in jail. Commitment No commitment no reward. Make sure your business partner is committed to the vision and mission. Ensure that they understand the choices they’ve made and are committed to seeing the company through to it’s logical endpoint—even if that’s returning investors money and shuttering the business. Commitment means the partner has clarity on their responsibilities. Commitment is accepting full responsibility for your decisions and actions. Get a partner that is at least as committed as you are. Relevant Experience Some relevant experience in your industry could be beneficial. It could also be detrimental. If you’re solving a hard problem it may be better to find a set of fresh eyes that can see the problem from a different angle. If you’re attacking an existing market in a new way the relationships and industry knowledge of an insider might help you achieve your objectives faster. Discipline A disciplined mind leads to happiness. You need a partner with a tremendous amount of discipline. Without discipline you won’t weather the storm.

Question: What websites, if any, provide historical airline ticket prices?
Answer: There’s really no great product out there that has historical price data that’s displayed visually or easily accessed via an API. Here’s some products that use historical information to try and provide data (and solve the exact problem you’re having) The Bureau of Transportation Statistics The BTS provides data on the average price of domestic flights. This is a good place to start if you’re just looking for raw data. I checked a few routes and the data goes back to 1995 and shows the average flight price each fiscal quarter. Google Flights - Tracked Prices and Alerts Go to the Google Flights homepage and click the menu icon on the top left hand side. From there choose “Tracked Prices.” You can track prices for routes and destinations but you can’t view the historical data beyond a very simple line chart. Hopper Hopper is an app that shows you when to fly and buy. It uses historical price data to tell you when prices are lowest and when the optimal time to buy it. You can setup alerts for multiple flights. There’s no charts or way to view or access data. FareCompare FareCompare has a value proposition similar to Hopper. They tell you when to fly and when to buy. They offer alerts and deals as well as booking capabilities. FareDetective Probably the product that meets your needs best. They provide a simple, Flash based graph that shows you average fares between destination and on specific routes over the previous twelve months. Question: How does target marketing compare to mass marketing?
Answer: In order to answer this question we need to clarify what you mean by “target marketing” and “mass marketing.” Target marketing is the identification and selection of a cross-section of the marketplace. It doesn’t matter if you’re selling product or services, or if you’re selling to consumers or businesses—target marketing generally means you’re attempting to reach a very specific and well defined group (AKA “market segment”) within a broader market. Presumable the group you target will have a distinct need for your product or service and your messaging, value proposition, brand strategy, packaging, pricing, and positioning will resonate with that audience. Target marketing is generally used when the approach to product and service development is inline with the strategy inherent to target marketing—that is the design, brand, and solutions offered by your product or service is specialized in nature and has a clear and unique use for a sub-set of a larger market or demographic. Therefore, target marketing and the product (or service) research and development, design, branding, packaging and positioning must all be create in harmony with one another. That is to say target marketing does not exist in a vacuum and is not a useful tactic. It’s a small piece of a larger puzzle of how a business communicates with it’s chosen customers, delivers value, and makes money. Mass marketing is the opposite approach. Mass marketing is the creation and design of a product or service to specifically appeal to a large, reachable, and generally homogenous (at least at the service level) audience. You may be well served by learning more about direct marketing vs. brand marketing.

Question: I am wondering any tips for marketing a paid SDK?
Answer: First you need to figure out who people will buy the product. Conduct user research and customer development. Start building buyer personas so you can understand (in your customer’s language) the real benefits of your product and the real problem(s) it solves. Use this knowledge to inform your strategy and craft compelling messaging that you can use in your advertisements, in your web copy, sales presentations, emails, etc. All of your marketing and sales collateral should be focused on communicating the distilled value of your product in simple, crystal clear terms. If that’s done—go find your customers. Where do they spend time? What media do they read? How do they learn about similar products and services? What do they all have in common? Start build a profile of the information your target market consumes to get better insight into the avenues you can use to get the attention of your target market. Ok so you know your customers, how they think, what they want, their vernacular, etc... Now figure out how they are currently addressing the problem you are solving…IE. who are your competitors? What’s their value proposition? Who are they marketing to and why? Dig deep into your competitor’s marketing strategy and tactics and try to figure out what’s working. If you find enough evidence to indicate a particular tactic or channel (HELLO SEO) is driving value then go ahead and copy it—make it better—provide as much value for your audience as possible—then execute like crazy. Ok so you know your audience, and your competitors. Time to look within. What’s your budget and time constraints? What are your goals and objectives? Make this part of your planning strategy so you can map your goals, objectives, and strategy to the tactics needed to get you there. Ok, the part you’re waiting for: get tactical. You have a lot of options for reaching developers online as they use their computers for > 8 hours per day and are generally power users of their mobile devices, tablets, etc. You should look at opportunities for driving inbound traffic through traditional content marketing and SEO—use the information you learned during customer development to address “top of the funnel” needs with your educational content. You should implement some basic retargeting, remarketing, and display tactics if you go the content marketing route—keep your core message in front of your audience. Get granular if there’s value there—if you’ve figured out customer segments with different needs tailor your content and display creative to speak to those needs (EG. tweak your ad copy). Partnerships could be a big opportunity. You need someone with an audience. Podcasts + blogs. Developers read blogs. They also listen to podcasts. You can sponsor or appear on popular blogs and podcasts to get your message out to your audience. Email lists—can you get a mention in an email list? Create a separate funnel (landing page, content piece) for that list that speaks to their needs—again tailor your messaging to the needs, hopes, dreams, and desires of the audience you’re marketing to. There’s thousands of tactics to choose from. But choosing the right ones depends on spending the time in the early stages to learn about your customers and your competitors so you can find the white space in the marketplace. Then you must have the discipline to methodically run tests, measure, evaluate, and iterate on your marketing tactics. This is the most important thing™. Good luck.

Question: How do social media agencies price?
Answer: Like all marketing agencies, there's a few pricing models social media marketing agencies use to price their services. 1. Fixed Scope / Fixed Bid If the client doesn't want to sign a long term contract, or is looking to ease into a relationship an agency may provide fixed bid, fixed scope pricing. In this model the client and agency work together to define a narrow set of deliverables and agreed upon scope and corresponding budget. The contract can be constrained by both scope and time. In many cases a contract may explicitly state things that are not included or may set guidelines for additional expenses or out-of-scope work. 2. Retainer Based / Resource Based Model The agency will charge a retainer and burn that retainer based on resources needed to execute the desired campaign. Each resource may have it's own concomitant rate (EG. Designer - $110/hr, Developer $135/hr). Or, in some cases an agency may use a single blended rate. 3. Productized Service Model / SaaS This model is normally employed at the lower end of the market (EG. for lower budget small businesses). This model simplifies and accelerates the buying and selling process by clearly defining and limiting the scope and deliverables of the project. In most cases only the highest priority services are provided. Sometimes this model is self-service, meaning the client will utilize a software application to accomplish their goals vs. utilizing a team of marketers and designers.

Question: What would be the best way to recruit specialist designers, developers, marketers, copy writers, etc. to 'register' to be part of a virtual agency?
Answer: You want to start by developing a recruiting pipeline and defining all of the processes and procedures needed to go from talent requirement definitions to on-boarding a new contractor. Let's walk through the process of developing a pipeline of designers. 1. Let's start with your needs. You've mentioned you need designers, developers, markets and copywriters. It's time to get specific. What type of designers do you want? What will they be designing? Do you need illustrators or someone to design a mobile app UI? Do you want a web designer or someone familiar with print? Will they need to do prototyping and mockups? What software skills should they have (Adobe CS, Balsamiq, Sketch, etc)? Will you need someone to do animation? Get as specific as possible on the roles and responsibilities needed (alternatively—utilize a broad definition here and find generalist designers). Put all the above in writing. If you want to recruit at scale you need to build an internal knowledgebase with all of the documents needed for the end-to-end process. Start now. Move as fast as possible to get v1.0 of this doc completed—you can improve it over time and as you learn what works and what doesn't. 2. Now, write an advertisement... Most job sites are the last place you want to go to find talent, but you still need to put this in writing. You have to sell your organization, it's mission/vision/values etc. Creatives want to work on fun projects, with other talented people. Be clear about the nature of the job—it's a contractor opportunity for freelancers. Specify a range of hours if possible. More detail is better. Include some filters in your advertisement–I'll cover that later. 3. Start building out the underlying infrastructure for managing the Talent Pipeline—before you need it. Again, don't spend a ton of time here, and don't try to reinvent the wheel. WP Curve has written about their workflow for hiring developers here: "Our exact process for hiring developers in the Philippines." They keep it simple and automate as much as possible. Don't waste a ton of money on fancy pants HR recruiting software unless compliance is your number one priority. Sometimes the simplest solution is the best (EG. Google Sheets). 4. Start recruiting. Go where the prospects are. If you're looking for designers, start in design communities like Dribble, Forrst, or Behance. Get active in online forums. Try not to use sites like Freelancer, Upwork, or Elance...Unless you're looking for very low quality $5 dollar design. Start building up your pipeline. Manage the process in Trello. 5. Develop your interviewing process. Try and standardize the interview process. From prospect communications to the toolset you use (skype, google hangouts, maybe an actual phone, etc). I won't go into to much detail here as many other have written about the interviewing process. 6. Develop your legal process. Make sure you have the appropriate documents, contracts, and necessary legal requirements taken care of. This will save you a lot of heartache in the long run. If you're a startup try to avoid hiring a lawyer who will simply copy and paste a bunch of boilerplate and spend 15 minutes customizing the document for you, then charge an obscene amount of money. 7. Develop your on-boarding process. What are the twelve steps you need to take to ensure a smooth and streamlined start to your relationship with a new contractor? This will be unique to your business and personal preferences. Document it. Improve it over time. 8. Ensure you have crystal clear communication. You should educate your new partner on your workflows, project management and communication processes. Put it in writing. Create a "freelancer resources" Trello board, blog post, or private Google Document. Send it along and ensure contractors read it before you begin working together. Communication is oxygen when working remotely. Having the resources contractors need to answer questions without reaching out to you or your team will save everyone a lot of time and empower external partners to get things done faster.

And if you're looking for a inbound marketing platform it's probably because your trying to solve a broader problems or achieve an overarching business goals—and you think inbound marketing software might help you do that. But let me be the first person to warn you: the software won't do the hardest parts of the process for you, it will just grease the wheels a bit and (hopefully) make your life easier. You still have to do all the hard work of choosing the right strategy, creating awesome content, having the right underlying technology stack, the right messaging, the right product/service, etc....So my advice would be to figure out everything else before you waste your time with inbound marketing software. Ask yourself this one question: If this inbound marketing software meets all of my needs and does everything I hope and wish it will do, it what way will my business look different in one year...Two years? Three years? One last thing—I'm bias. I prefer to build a customized solution that uniquely meets my needs. I find most of the "all-in-one" marketing platforms to be just that—jack of all trades software that over simplifies a complex thing, and in doing so reduces the amount of flexibility and customization you can implement. My approach is to find the best tool for each need and layer that on top of my stack as needed. Now...onto the evaluation. Inbound Marketing platforms on the whole combine a few different features: 1. Measurement, analytics, and reporting features for your digital channels. 2. Email marketing. 3. List management / database management / CRM. 4. Marketing automation features. 5. Landing page hosting, creation, and testing. 6. They claim to offer SEO features, but let's be honest, they don't compare to MOZ / SEMRush, AHREFS, etc... 7. And sometimes they offer sales tools (like HubSpot CRM / Sidekick) as an add-on. Phew, that's a lot of stuff in one piece of software. And it'll cost ya a pretty penny. One that I would recommend you invest in Paid Advertising if you don't already have a mature business, a war chest of content, and a team of people to implement, integrate, and grow the platform. So here's the main players in the space: HubSpot, who seems to have coined the term "inbound marketing" which is really just a spin on a marketing techniques that's as old as marketing itself. Pardot, the enterprise player. Eloqua, also an enterprise player. Marketo, marketing automation player. InfusionSoft, a small business player, which seems to have focused on the info marketing space for a long time. Ontraport, also a small business player. My recommendation...unless you're ready, don't invest in a marketing automation platform. Just use MailChimp for email marketing (or another option that has some automation features) and a free CRM like HubSpot...Then when you're ready, move on to the expensive software mentioned above. Good luck.

Question: What is the best lifestyle data to use for Buyer Personas?
Answer: Excellent question. Allow me to offer a surprising answer: lifestyle data is part of a buyer profile, not a persona. A buyer profile is data-heavy archetype of your typical target prospect, but it doesn't tell us anything about how your target prospects make a decision or purchase....And that's what a buyer persona does. But it could be used to build a customer profile, which is completely different. A persona is a complete picture of the wants, needs, desire, and fears of your target audience....and specific a small segment of that audience (a persona). A persona should cover: 1. The most important reasons prospects choose to buy one thing over another, or how they prioritize features, options, pricing, payment etc. 2. The results or outcomes that the prospects expects from purchasing a product or solution. In other words—the value they are looking for from your product or service, in their own words. 3. The objections, obstacles and barriers to purchasing. What prevents one particular buyer persona from buying? 4. The journey a persona takes during the decision making process. How does one evaluate options, compare competitors and make the final decision? 5. Decision making criteria—the specific attributes that your prospect uses to evaluate and compare their options. So while demographic and psychographic data are useful in determining who your prospects are, they are not buyer personas.

Question: Anyone has master thesis topic that is related in social media, neuromarketing or inbound marketing? Which journal us the best to read and analyze?
Answer: You've mentioned three very broad disciplines. I'll address social media and inbound for you. Neuro-marketing will require it's own question and answer. If you want to learn about social media, the best thing you can do is study organization that are really good at it. What does good mean? Well, to 5 organizations it could mean 5 different things. One company may be focused on building an audience. So they might be good at creating interesting content, distributing that content via paid and organic social media marketing, and attracting new users to their page/profile. Study the strategies and tactics they use. Copy them. Try them on your own. Understand that every vertical is different, and within each vertical there are customers at different phases of the customer journey (IE. personas). Know that there is no silver bullet. Other companies may use social media to generate leads. These people are probably direct marketers. They know their numbers. They analyze and optimize for CPM, CPC, CTR, Conversions, ROAS, CLTV, and potentially a slew of other metrics....They look at the end-to-end funnel and try to connect the dots—they have a singular goal of driving more leads...Good direct marketers identify the levers that generate results and are laser focused on optimizing these critical few factors. Company #3 may be drinking the "awareness" or "engagement" kool-aide. If you're a consultant, go sell stuff to these people. They will pay for inputs and not worry about results. They engage in "brand marketing," for the sake of "brand marketing." Crawl inside the head of this person and understand what motivates them (ego? notoriety? popularity?)...Understand the difference between company #1 and company #2...Be careful about replicating their strategy unless you have very deep pockets and a seemingly limitless budget. Inbound Marketing While this is a relatively new term inbound marketing has been around for ages. The idea is that you provide useful, educational content to your target market...Inbound is executed at various levels of sophistication and investment. Company #1 pays $20 for a 500 word article on a subject they think their market is interested in. They post it to their blog. They do this once or twice per week. They don't measure anything. They have no plan, or a very vague plan with something like "post twice per week" as the objective. This is the lowest level of inbound marketing sophistication. Company #2 is a little smarter, and has more resources. They know that they have to write content that search engine are interested in....So they do some basic keyword research in Google Ad Planner. The look at what their competitors are doing. They ask a member of the sales team what common questions prospects are asking...Then they take that information and have the intern develop 3 pieces of content per week...They post it to their blog and check google analytics once a month to see if it's generating any traffic. They stop doing it after 7 months because they don't think its working. Company #3 used to be company #1, and company #2...But they kept going, and they found help outside of their organization. They convinced their CFO to allocate the resources they need. They started this process by analyzing what went wrong with their previous inbound marketing campaigns. Then, they interviewed customers and prospects. They figured out why people shop, and how they shop. They crawled inside the mind of their prospects to uncover their hopes, fears, and desires. They string together their knowledge to develop customer personas and a unique customer decision journey. They research the competition, and they use quantitative methods to evaluate their own company's progress against the competition. They try to identify gaps, weaknesses, and opportunities to distance their co. from the competition. They don't just do keyword research. They have a finely tuned process for finding and evaluating keyword opportunities. They predict traffic levels, costs, share of voice, and they look at the organic and paid search opportunity. They select long tail keywords to target, and map each to a buyer person / need state...then they map that to the content on their website. Company #3 knows numbers matter. They've implemented measurement plans and have installed and setup their analytics packages (and audited them to ensure the data is accurate). They have a reporting process and have identified measures of success. They've been down the wrong path before and are determined to justify their investment–and prove its worth. They've setup marketing automation capabilities for visitors that don't immediately convert to leads. They've created granular retargeting and remarketing campaigns that speak to the specific problem that brought visitors to their website....And they iterate on this complete process over and over again until their marketplace.

Question: Software-as-a-Service (SaaS): What is the best way to hire and build a small SDR (sales development representative) Team?
Answer: I just did this. Here's the process I used: 1. Recruit talent. Being an SDR is challenging. It's a grind. You need to find people that can thrive in the SDR role...So you need a solid process for recruiting, filtering, and hiring the best talent. There's plenty of articles out there on this subject so I won't go into detail. In my experience the best talent I've found almost always comes from another business with an under-appreciated employee, the diamond in the rough so to speak. 2. Onboarding You need to get SDRs up to speed as fast as humanly possible. Every hour they are not prospecting for your organization is a wasted hour. Get a solid onboarding process in place before you start recruiting to avoid this. 3. Training A subset of the onboarding process—while every employee should have some sort of onboarding/orientation, SDRs get a unique training track that helps them understand the product/service they are selling, their target customer(s), personas and their needs, etc. I like to start with a holistic high level view of the marketplace and progress into the nitty gritty of the sales process, marketing stack (tools), email templates, copywriting/persuasion basics, etc. Be sure you cover handling objections and provide your SDRs with some "cheat sheets" as a reference. Ensure you implement some form of education system that tests their abilities (quiz / elearning / etc). Provide a visual overview of the entire process (including what comes before SDRs and after them). Ask SDRs for ways to improve the process. Value their feedback. Allow new SDRs to observe your best people. 4. Metrics + Dashboards You need to have crystal clear, simple metrics that SDRs are accountable too. Ensure you have a process for compiling the data, and if avoidable, don't make the SDRs compile the data on their own—it's a waste of their time. Metrics should be based on your objectives. If you're doing outbound email prospecting with an objective to get a phone appointment use some simple metrics like delivery, open, CTR, reply rate, appt. conversion rate, etc. 5. Cadence / Process You need a process. It must be repeatable. It must be easy to train. It must be part of your CRM / lead management / marketing automation or other software tool. I've seen people use Trello. I've seen people use Excel. Use whatever works but be mindful of the need to make this process quantifiable. Ask your SDRs what could be improved. Map out the entire process and explain it during #3 above. Ensure the cadence is congruent with your company's values. 6. Automate, iterate, repeat. This is a work in progress. Improve the process over time. Automate as much as possible. Start building your internal playbook. Update the playbook in parallel with your recruiting, onboarding and training process. Don't tell anyone else how you're generating all those leads ;).

Question: What's the best envelope for a direct mail campaign?
Answer: The answer is, I don't know and neither does anyone else. Direct mail is finicky, like all marketing. There's so many variables at play (weather, niche, day of week, time of year, etc) that you have to test, test, and test some more. And don't forget to measure! Be sure to run a control against whatever your testing. Try crazy, creative ideas. Also, don't rely on really small batches, your tests must be statistically significant. Measure. Measure everything. When testing, control for as many factors are under your control (don't sort a list by zip code and then split it in half, sort alphabetically and extract alternate rows for example). Use call tracking phone numbers. Call Fire, IfByPhone, CallRail, etc. Know your response rates. The sole purpose of your envelope should be to: 1. avoid the trash bin / junk pile 2. get the marketing message opened A lot of people will tell you bigger is better, or "put some graphics on it." ...Guess what? They may be right, or they may be wrong...Unless they've recently mailed to your particular list, with a similar offer then they don't know. Listen, let them provide you with creative ideas that can have idea sex, but never buy their answers as facts. Its non-sense. If you're looking for ideas that will stand out, read "Outrageous Marketing" by Dan Kennedy and his partner Bill. Check out copy doodles. Read Robert Collier.  That's it.
